course.title: French, Start to Fluent
course.subtitle: Metropolitan French from real-world basics through fluent, everyday command — real sentences, real grammar, real conversation
course.heroLedeSuffix: Real sentences from lesson one, with genuine native-quality audio for every single line.

a2-present-er.title: Present Tense: -ER Verbs, Être, and Avoir
a2-present-er.pattern: je -e, tu -es, il/elle -e, nous -ons, vous -ez, ils/elles -ent
a2-present-er.explanation: Most French verbs end in -er (parler, manger, habiter) and follow one regular pattern: drop -er, add -e/-es/-e/-ons/-ez/-ent. "Être" (to be) and "avoir" (to have) are irregular and used constantly: je suis/j'ai, tu es/tu as, il est/il a, nous sommes/nous avons, vous êtes/vous avez, ils sont/ils ont.
a2-present-er.fact: "Avoir" is used in many expressions where English uses "to be": "avoir faim" (to be hungry, literally "to have hunger"), "avoir soif" (to be thirsty), "avoir raison" (to be right), "avoir vingt ans" (to be twenty years old).

dialogue.native: Tu parles très bien français !
dialogue.en: You speak French very well!

dialogue.native: Merci, j'habite ici depuis deux ans.
dialogue.en: Thanks, I've lived here for two years.

a2-ir-re-aller-faire.title: -IR/-RE Verbs, and Two Key Irregulars: Aller, Faire
a2-ir-re-aller-faire.explanation: Regular -ir verbs (finir, choisir) add -is/-is/-it/-issons/-issez/-issent. Regular -re verbs (vendre, attendre) add -s/-s/[nothing]/-ons/-ez/-ent. Two irregular verbs are essential from day one: "aller" (to go: vais/vas/va/allons/allez/vont) and "faire" (to do/make: fais/fais/fait/faisons/faites/font) — both used constantly in everyday speech and in set expressions.
a2-ir-re-aller-faire.fact: "Faire" appears in dozens of common expressions where English uses a completely different verb: "faire les courses" (to go grocery shopping), "faire du sport" (to play sports), "faire attention" (to pay attention), "faire beau/mauvais" (to be nice/bad weather).

dialogue.native: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
dialogue.en: What are you doing this weekend?

dialogue.native: Je vais faire du sport et finir mes devoirs.
dialogue.en: I'm going to play sports and finish my homework.

a2-gender-agreement.title: Gender and Agreement: Nouns, Articles, and Adjectives
a2-gender-agreement.explanation: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, and articles and adjectives must agree: "le grand livre" (the big book, masc.), "la grande maison" (the big house, fem. — adjective gains an -e), "les grands livres"/"les grandes maisons" (plural, gains -s). Many adjectives change more irregularly in the feminine: "beau"→"belle", "nouveau"→"nouvelle", "blanc"→"blanche".
a2-gender-agreement.fact: Gender is mostly unpredictable and simply has to be memorized with each noun — but a few endings are strong hints: words ending in -tion, -sion, -té, -ette are almost always feminine ("la nation", "la beauté"), while words ending in -age, -ment, -eau are usually masculine ("le mariage", "le gouvernement").

dialogue.native: Cette nouvelle robe est vraiment belle.
dialogue.en: This new dress is really beautiful.

dialogue.native: Merci, et j'aime beaucoup ton nouveau manteau aussi.
dialogue.en: Thanks, and I really like your new coat too.

a2-reflexive.title: Reflexive Verbs: Actions Done to Oneself
a2-reflexive.explanation: Reflexive verbs describe an action the subject does to itself, and need a reflexive pronoun that matches the subject before the verb: "je me lève" (I get up, literally "I raise myself"), "tu te laves" (you wash yourself), "il se réveille" (he wakes up), "nous nous habillons" (we get dressed). Many everyday routine verbs in French are reflexive even when their English translation isn't.
a2-reflexive.fact: In the negative, "ne" goes before the reflexive pronoun and "pas" after the verb: "je ne me lève pas" (I don't get up) — the reflexive pronoun stays glued to the verb, not to "ne".

dialogue.native: Tu te lèves à quelle heure le matin ?
dialogue.en: What time do you get up in the morning?

dialogue.native: Je me réveille vers sept heures, puis je me douche.
dialogue.en: I wake up around seven, then I shower.

a2-passe-compose-avoir.title: Passé Composé: Talking About the Past with Avoir
a2-passe-compose-avoir.explanation: Most French verbs form their compound past tense with a present-tense form of "avoir" plus a past participle: "j'ai parlé" (I spoke/have spoken), "tu as fini" (you finished), "il a vendu" (he sold). Regular participles follow the verb ending: -er → -é, -ir → -i, -re → -u. This is the everyday past tense in spoken French — far more common than any literary past tense.
a2-passe-compose-avoir.fact: Many extremely common verbs have irregular participles that must be memorized: "avoir" → "eu", "être" → "été", "faire" → "fait", "voir" → "vu", "prendre" → "pris", "dire" → "dit", "écrire" → "écrit", "boire" → "bu".

dialogue.native: Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ce week-end ?
dialogue.en: What did you do this weekend?

dialogue.native: J'ai vu un film et j'ai lu un bon livre.
dialogue.en: I saw a movie and I read a good book.

a2-passe-compose-etre.title: Passé Composé with Être: Movement and Change Verbs
a2-passe-compose-etre.pattern: être (present) + past participle, agreeing in gender/number with the subject
a2-passe-compose-etre.explanation: About a dozen verbs — mostly involving movement or a change of state — use "être" instead of "avoir" in the passé composé, and their past participle must AGREE with the subject's gender and number: "il est allé" / "elle est allée" / "ils sont allés" / "elles sont allées". Common être-verbs: aller (go), venir (come), arriver (arrive), partir (leave), entrer (enter), sortir (exit), monter (go up), descendre (go down), naître (be born), mourir (die), rester (stay), tomber (fall).
a2-passe-compose-etre.fact: All reflexive verbs also use "être" in the passé composé, and generally agree the same way: "elle s'est levée" (she got up) — the -e is added because "elle" is feminine, even though "lever" itself doesn't take être when non-reflexive ("j'ai levé la main" — I raised my hand, uses avoir).

dialogue.native: Tu es arrivée à quelle heure hier soir ?
dialogue.en: What time did you arrive last night?

dialogue.native: Je suis rentrée vers minuit, un peu tard.
dialogue.en: I got home around midnight, a bit late.

a2-imparfait.title: Imparfait: Describing the Past — Habits and Background
a2-imparfait.explanation: The imperfect describes ongoing states, habits, and background scenery in the past — not a single completed event. Form it by taking the "nous" form of the present tense, dropping "-ons", and adding: -ais/-ais/-ait/-ions/-iez/-aient. "Nous parlons" → "je parlais" (I used to speak / I was speaking). "Être" is the only irregular stem: "j'étais", "tu étais", "il était"...
a2-imparfait.fact: The passé composé and imparfait are often used together in the same sentence, each doing a different job: the imparfait sets the scene ("il pleuvait" — it was raining) while the passé composé reports what happened in that scene ("quand je suis sorti" — when I went out): "Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti" (It was raining when I went out).

dialogue.native: Qu'est-ce que tu faisais quand j'ai appelé ?
dialogue.en: What were you doing when I called?

dialogue.native: Je regardais la télévision, il pleuvait dehors.
dialogue.en: I was watching television, it was raining outside.

a2-futur-proche.title: Futur Proche: The Near Future with Aller
a2-futur-proche.explanation: The easiest way to talk about the future in French is the "futur proche" (near future): a present-tense form of "aller" plus an infinitive: "je vais partir" (I'm going to leave), "elle va manger" (she's going to eat), "nous allons voyager" (we're going to travel). It works exactly like English "going to" and is far more common in everyday speech than the simple future tense.
a2-futur-proche.fact: In the negative, "ne...pas" wraps around the conjugated "aller", not the infinitive: "je ne vais pas partir" (I'm not going to leave) — the infinitive itself always stays untouched at the end.

dialogue.native: Qu'est-ce que vous allez faire ce soir ?
dialogue.en: What are you going to do tonight?

dialogue.native: On va dîner au restaurant, puis on va voir un film.
dialogue.en: We're going to have dinner at a restaurant, then we're going to see a movie.

a2-object-pronouns.title: Object Pronouns: Le/La/Les and Lui/Leur
a2-object-pronouns.pattern: direct: le/la/les (replace things/people) · indirect: lui/leur (replace "à + person")
a2-object-pronouns.explanation: Direct object pronouns replace a noun that directly receives the action, with no preposition: "le"/"la"/"les" (him/her/it/them) — "Je vois le livre" → "Je le vois". Indirect object pronouns replace "à + person": "lui" (to him/her) and "leur" (to them) — "Je parle à Marie" → "Je lui parle". Both types go directly BEFORE the conjugated verb, unlike English where the pronoun follows the verb.
a2-object-pronouns.fact: "Le", "la", and "les" also famously double as definite articles ("the") — context always makes clear which role they're playing, since articles precede nouns while pronouns precede verbs.

dialogue.native: Tu as vu mon frère récemment ?
dialogue.en: Have you seen my brother recently?

dialogue.native: Oui, je l'ai vu hier, et je lui ai parlé de toi.
dialogue.en: Yes, I saw him yesterday, and I talked to him about you.

a2-comparatives.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
a2-comparatives.pattern: plus/moins/aussi + adjective + que · le/la/les plus/moins + adjective
a2-comparatives.explanation: Comparisons use "plus...que" (more...than), "moins...que" (less...than), and "aussi...que" (as...as): "Elle est plus grande que moi" (She's taller than me), "Ce livre est moins cher que l'autre" (This book is cheaper than the other one). Superlatives add the definite article: "le plus grand" (the tallest), "la moins chère" (the least expensive).
a2-comparatives.fact: "Bon" (good) and "mauvais" (bad) have irregular comparative forms just like English "good/better/best": "bon" → "meilleur" (better) → "le meilleur" (the best), never "plus bon". "Mauvais" can go either way: "pire"/"le pire" (more common, more emphatic) or the regular "plus mauvais".

dialogue.native: Ce restaurant est meilleur que l'autre, non ?
dialogue.en: This restaurant is better than the other one, right?

dialogue.native: Oui, et c'est le meilleur du quartier, je pense.
dialogue.en: Yes, and I think it's the best in the neighborhood.

b1-imperative.title: Imperative: Giving Commands
b1-imperative.pattern: tu/nous/vous forms of the present tense, minus the subject pronoun
b1-imperative.explanation: The imperative just drops the subject pronoun from the tu/nous/vous present-tense forms: "Parle !" (Speak!, tu), "Parlons !" (Let's speak!, nous), "Parlez !" (Speak!, vous). One quirk: -er verbs (and "aller") drop the final -s from the tu form: "tu parles" → "Parle !" not "Parles !". Negative commands wrap "ne...pas" around the verb as usual: "Ne parle pas !" (Don't speak!).
b1-imperative.fact: "Être", "avoir", and "savoir" have irregular imperatives borrowed from their subjunctive stems: "sois/soyons/soyez" (be), "aie/ayons/ayez" (have), "sache/sachons/sachez" (know) — these don't follow the normal drop-the-pronoun rule at all.

dialogue.native: Sois patient, ça va bientôt arriver !
dialogue.en: Be patient, it's going to arrive soon!

dialogue.native: D'accord, mais dépêchons-nous quand même un peu.
dialogue.en: Okay, but let's still hurry a little.

b1-subjunctive-intro.title: Present Subjunctive: Wishes, Wants, and Necessity
b1-subjunctive-intro.explanation: When one person wants or needs another to do something, French switches the second verb into the subjunctive after "que": "Je veux que tu viennes" (I want you to come), "Il faut que nous partions" (We need to leave). Most subjunctive stems come from the "ils" present-tense form minus -ent, plus these endings: -e/-es/-e/-ions/-iez/-ent. "Nous"/"vous" forms often match the imperfect instead.
b1-subjunctive-intro.fact: "Il faut que" (it is necessary that) is one of the most common subjunctive triggers in everyday French, used constantly for obligations: "Il faut que je parte" (I have to leave) — far more common in speech than the more formal "il est nécessaire que".

dialogue.native: Il faut que tu finisses ce travail aujourd'hui.
dialogue.en: You need to finish this work today.

dialogue.native: Je sais, je veux juste qu'on m'aide un peu.
dialogue.en: I know, I just want someone to help me a little.

b1-relative-clauses.title: Relative Clauses: Connecting Ideas with Qui, Que, Où, Dont
b1-relative-clauses.pattern: qui (subject) · que (object) · où (place/time) · dont (of/about which, replaces de + noun)
b1-relative-clauses.explanation: "Qui" replaces the SUBJECT of the relative clause: "la femme qui parle" (the woman who is speaking). "Que" replaces the OBJECT: "le livre que je lis" (the book that I'm reading). "Où" replaces a place or time: "la ville où je suis né" (the city where I was born). "Dont" replaces anything introduced by "de": "le livre dont je parle" (the book I'm talking about, from "parler de").
b1-relative-clauses.fact: Unlike English, French never drops the relative pronoun — English allows "the book I read" with no "that," but French always requires "le livre que j'ai lu", "que" can never be omitted.

dialogue.native: C'est la ville où j'ai grandi.
dialogue.en: This is the city where I grew up.

dialogue.native: Et qui est cette personne dont tu me parlais l'autre jour ?
dialogue.en: And who is that person you were telling me about the other day?

b1-time-expressions.title: Depuis, Pendant, Il y a: Talking About Duration
b1-time-expressions.pattern: depuis + present tense (ongoing) · pendant + duration (completed span) · il y a + time (ago)
b1-time-expressions.explanation: "Depuis" (since/for) pairs with the PRESENT tense for something still ongoing: "J'habite ici depuis trois ans" (I've lived here for three years — and still do). "Pendant" (for/during) describes a completed span, often with the passé composé: "J'ai vécu à Lyon pendant trois ans" (I lived in Lyon for three years — no longer). "Il y a" (ago) marks a point in the past: "Je suis arrivé il y a trois ans" (I arrived three years ago).
b1-time-expressions.fact: This depuis-with-present pattern is a classic difference from English, where "I have lived here for three years" uses a perfect tense — French uses the simple present because, from the speaker's perspective, the action is still happening right now.

dialogue.native: Tu habites à Paris depuis combien de temps ?
dialogue.en: How long have you lived in Paris?

dialogue.native: J'y habite depuis cinq ans, mais avant j'ai vécu à Nice pendant deux ans.
dialogue.en: I've lived here for five years, but before that I lived in Nice for two years.

b1-plus-que-parfait.title: Plus-que-parfait: An Action Before Another Past Action
b1-plus-que-parfait.explanation: The plus-que-parfait describes something that had already happened before another point in the past: "Quand je suis arrivé, ils avaient déjà commencé" (when I arrived, they had already started). It's built with the IMPERFECT of "avoir" or "être" plus the past participle — the same auxiliary-choice and agreement rules as the passé composé, just with the auxiliary itself pushed one step further into the past.
b1-plus-que-parfait.fact: This tense is what lets you clearly sequence two past events in a story — without it, "j'ai perdu mes clés que j'avais achetées" (I lost the keys I had bought) would collapse into ambiguous timing about which event came first.

dialogue.native: Quand nous sommes arrivés au cinéma, le film avait déjà commencé.
dialogue.en: When we got to the movies, the film had already started.

dialogue.native: Quel dommage ! Je n'étais jamais arrivé aussi en retard.
dialogue.en: What a shame! I had never arrived so late.

b1plus-futur-simple.title: Simple Future: What Will Happen
b1plus-futur-simple.explanation: The simple future attaches endings directly onto the infinitive (dropping the final -e for -re verbs): "je parlerai" (I will speak), "tu finiras" (you will finish), "elle vendra" (she will sell). It's used for predictions, formal plans, and polite commands, and sounds slightly more formal/definitive than the futur proche ("aller" + infinitive) used constantly in casual speech.
b1plus-futur-simple.fact: About twenty common verbs have an irregular future stem while keeping the regular endings: "être" → "ser-", "avoir" → "aur-", "aller" → "ir-", "faire" → "fer-", "pouvoir" → "pourr-", "vouloir" → "voudr-", "venir" → "viendr-", "voir" → "verr-" — so "je serai", "j'aurai", "j'irai", etc.

dialogue.native: Tu crois qu'il pleuvra demain ?
dialogue.en: Do you think it will rain tomorrow?

dialogue.native: Je ne sais pas, mais je prendrai un parapluie au cas où.
dialogue.en: I don't know, but I'll bring an umbrella just in case.

b1plus-conditionnel.title: Conditional Tense: What Would Happen
b1plus-conditionnel.explanation: The conditional uses the exact same stems as the future (including the same irregulars) but swaps in the imperfect-style -ais endings: "je parlerais" (I would speak), "j'aurais" (I would have), "je ferais" (I would do). It expresses hypothetical actions, polite requests, and past-projected future ("il a dit qu'il viendrait" — he said he would come).
b1plus-conditionnel.fact: "Je voudrais" (I would like) is the single most common conditional phrase in everyday French — softer and more polite than "je veux" (I want), exactly like English "I would like" versus "I want": always the first phrase taught for ordering in a restaurant.

dialogue.native: Que ferais-tu à ma place ?
dialogue.en: What would you do in my place?

dialogue.native: Je lui parlerais directement, ce serait le plus honnête.
dialogue.en: I would talk to them directly, it would be the most honest thing.

b1plus-passive.title: Passive Voice: When the Subject Receives the Action
b1plus-passive.pattern: être + past participle (agrees in gender/number), often + par + agent
b1plus-passive.explanation: The passive voice uses "être" plus a past participle that AGREES with the subject: "La lettre a été écrite par Anne" (The letter was written by Anne), "Les prix seront annoncés demain" (The prizes will be announced tomorrow). The agent, when mentioned, follows "par" (by). French uses the passive somewhat less than English — when there's no need to name who did the action, French often prefers the impersonal "on" instead: "On parle français ici" (French is spoken here) rather than a true passive construction.
b1plus-passive.fact: "On" is everywhere in spoken French as an all-purpose way to avoid the passive or a specific subject: "On m'a dit que..." (I was told that...), "Ici, on ne fume pas" (Smoking isn't allowed here) — native speakers reach for "on" far more often than a formal passive construction in casual conversation.

dialogue.native: Est-ce que les cartes de crédit sont acceptées ici ?
dialogue.en: Are credit cards accepted here?

dialogue.native: Je crois que oui, mais le menu a été mis à jour la semaine dernière, mieux vaut demander.
dialogue.en: I think so, but the menu was updated last week, better ask.

b1plus-discours-indirect.title: Indirect Speech: Reporting What Someone Said
b1plus-discours-indirect.pattern: dire/demander que + [reported clause, tense shifted back one step]
b1plus-discours-indirect.explanation: When you report what someone said from a past-tense perspective, the verb tense usually shifts back one step: present becomes imperfect ("J'ai faim" → il a dit qu'il avait faim), passé composé becomes plus-que-parfait ("J'ai fini" → il a dit qu'il avait fini), future becomes conditional ("Je viendrai" → il a dit qu'il viendrait). Yes/no questions use "si": "il m'a demandé si je viendrais" (he asked me if I would come); other questions keep their question word: "il m'a demandé où j'habitais" (he asked me where I lived).
b1plus-discours-indirect.fact: If the reporting verb is in the present tense ("il dit que..."), no tense shift happens at all — the shift only occurs when reporting from a past-tense perspective ("il a dit que..."), because that's when the original statement's "now" has already moved into the past.

dialogue.native: Qu'est-ce que le médecin t'a dit ?
dialogue.en: What did the doctor tell you?

dialogue.native: Il m'a dit de me reposer et de revenir si je n'allais pas mieux.
dialogue.en: He told me to rest and to come back if I didn't get better.

b2-si-clauses-present.title: Si-Clauses: Hypothetical Present
b2-si-clauses-present.explanation: For a hypothetical or contrary-to-fact PRESENT situation, use "si" + imperfect in the "si" clause, and the conditional in the result: "Si j'avais le temps, j'irais" (If I had time, I would go — but I don't). This contrasts with a real, open possibility, which uses "si" + present indicative + future or present: "Si j'ai le temps, j'irai" (If I have time, I'll go — genuinely possible).
b2-si-clauses-present.fact: Never use the conditional in the "si" clause itself — that's a common learner error copied from English "if I would have." French strictly separates the two halves: "si" always takes an indicative tense (present or imperfect), the conditional only ever appears in the result clause.

dialogue.native: Si tu avais plus de temps libre, que ferais-tu ?
dialogue.en: If you had more free time, what would you do?

dialogue.native: Je voyagerais sans doute beaucoup plus.
dialogue.en: I would probably travel a lot more.

b2-si-clauses-past.title: Si-Clauses: The Unreal Past
b2-si-clauses-past.explanation: For a hypothetical situation that DIDN'T actually happen in the past, go one step further back: "si" + plus-que-parfait in the "si" clause, with the conditionnel passé ("aurais"/"serais" + past participle) in the result: "Si j'avais su, je serais venu" (If I had known, I would have come — but I didn't know, and I didn't come). This is the classic structure for expressing regret or an alternate past.
b2-si-clauses-past.fact: Mixed-time sentences are common and natural: a past cause can produce a PRESENT hypothetical result — "Si j'avais accepté ce poste, je vivrais maintenant à Londres" (If I had accepted that job, I would now be living in London) — pairing plus-que-parfait with the plain conditionnel présent, not conditionnel passé, because the result describes now, not then.

dialogue.native: Si j'avais étudié davantage, j'aurais réussi l'examen.
dialogue.en: If I had studied more, I would have passed the exam.

dialogue.native: Eh bien, si tu t'entraînais un peu chaque jour maintenant, tu n'aurais pas ce problème la prochaine fois.
dialogue.en: Well, if you practiced a little each day now, you wouldn't have this problem next time.

b2-subjonctif-adverbial.title: Subjunctive After Adverbial Connectors
b2-subjonctif-adverbial.pattern: bien que/pour que/avant que/à moins que/jusqu'à ce que + subjunctive
b2-subjonctif-adverbial.explanation: Certain connectors always trigger the subjunctive because they introduce something not yet realized or hypothetical: "bien que" (although) — "Bien que ce soit difficile, j'essaie"; "pour que" (so that) — "Je te l'explique pour que tu comprennes"; "avant que" (before) — "Appelle avant qu'il ne soit trop tard"; "à moins que" (unless) — "Je n'irai pas à moins que tu ne viennes"; "jusqu'à ce que" (until) — "Attends jusqu'à ce qu'il arrive."
b2-subjonctif-adverbial.fact: "Avant que" and "à moins que" often carry an optional, purely stylistic "ne" (the "ne explétif") that adds no negative meaning at all: "avant qu'il ne parte" means exactly the same thing as "avant qu'il parte" — it's a formal-register habit, not a real negation.

dialogue.native: Bien qu'il pleuve, nous allons à la plage.
dialogue.en: Even though it's raining, we're going to the beach.

dialogue.native: Pourvu qu'il fasse beau plus tard, ce serait parfait.
dialogue.en: I hope the sun comes out later, it would be perfect.

b2-advanced-connectors.title: Advanced Connectors: Linking Ideas Like a Native Speaker
b2-advanced-connectors.pattern: cependant/néanmoins (however) · par conséquent/donc (therefore) · malgré (despite) · étant donné que/puisque (since/given that)
b2-advanced-connectors.explanation: These connectors let you build more sophisticated arguments. Contrast: "cependant" and "néanmoins" both mean "however," typically starting a new sentence. Consequence: "par conséquent" and the everyday "donc" mean "therefore/so." Concession: "malgré" (despite) is followed directly by a NOUN, not a clause: "malgré la pluie" (despite the rain). Cause: "étant donné que" and "puisque" (since/given that) introduce a reason the listener likely already knows, softer than a blunt "parce que".
b2-advanced-connectors.fact: "Néanmoins" and "cependant" are largely interchangeable, but "néanmoins" skews slightly more formal/written — common in academic or legal French, while "cependant" is the everyday default in both speech and writing.

dialogue.native: Le vol a eu trois heures de retard ; cependant, nous sommes arrivés à temps pour le mariage.
dialogue.en: The flight was delayed three hours; however, we arrived in time for the wedding.

dialogue.native: Quelle chance, puisque le mariage commençait à dix-huit heures pile.
dialogue.en: What luck, since the wedding started at six sharp.

b2-subjonctif-passe.title: Past Subjunctive and the Literary Imperfect Subjunctive
b2-subjonctif-passe.pattern: subjonctif passé: avoir/être (subjunctive) + participle · imparfait du subjonctif: literary only, recognize don't produce
b2-subjonctif-passe.explanation: The subjonctif passé expresses a completed action still governed by a subjunctive trigger: "Je suis content qu'il ait réussi" (I'm glad he succeeded — succeeding happened before the feeling). It's built with the PRESENT subjunctive of "avoir"/"être" plus the past participle. Separately, literary French has an "imparfait du subjonctif" (e.g. "qu'il fût", "qu'il eût") that survives only in very formal writing and classic literature — modern spoken French always replaces it with the present subjunctive, but recognizing it when reading is valuable.
b2-subjonctif-passe.fact: In 19th-century novels you'll see forms like "Il fallait qu'il partît" (he had to leave) where modern French would simply say "Il fallait qu'il parte" — the imparfait du subjonctif has essentially vanished from speech but its distinctive circumflex-accented forms are a hallmark of classic literary style.

b2plus-participle-agreement.title: Past Participle Agreement: The Full Picture
b2plus-participle-agreement.pattern: avoir + preceding direct object → agrees · être (non-reflexive) → agrees with subject · reflexive → agrees with reflexive pronoun if it's the direct object
b2plus-participle-agreement.explanation: With "avoir", the participle normally stays unchanged — UNLESS a direct object comes BEFORE the verb, in which case it agrees with that object: "J'ai vu la maison" (no preceding object, no agreement) vs "La maison que j'ai vue" ("que" refers to "la maison", which comes first, so "vue" gets the -e). With reflexive verbs, the participle agrees with the reflexive pronoun ONLY when that pronoun is the direct object: "Elle s'est lavée" (she washed herself — "se" is the direct object, agrees) but "Elle s'est lavé les mains" (she washed her hands — "les mains" is the direct object, "se" is indirect, so NO agreement).
b2plus-participle-agreement.fact: This is widely considered one of the most difficult rules in French grammar, and even educated native speakers sometimes get it wrong in casual writing — the Académie française itself has occasionally proposed simplifying it, so don't be discouraged if it takes real practice to feel automatic.

b2plus-compound-tenses.title: Compound Tenses Together: The Full Perfect System
b2plus-compound-tenses.pattern: j'ai/j'avais/j'aurai/j'aurais parlé — present/past/future/conditional perfect, all built the same way
b2plus-compound-tenses.explanation: French has a full family of compound tenses, all built the same way (avoir/être + past participle), just with the auxiliary itself in a different tense: passé composé "j'ai parlé" (I spoke), plus-que-parfait "j'avais parlé" (I had spoken), futur antérieur "j'aurai parlé" (I will have spoken, by some future point), conditionnel passé "j'aurais parlé" (I would have spoken). Once you know the participle and the auxiliary choice, all four tenses are just a matter of conjugating "avoir"/"être" correctly.
b2plus-compound-tenses.fact: The futur antérieur also has a probability use just like the simple future: "Ils seront déjà arrivés" doesn't just mean "they will have already arrived" — in casual speech it often means "they've probably already arrived," a guess about a completed action, not a genuine future prediction.

b2plus-nominalization.title: Nominalization: Turning Verbs and Adjectives into Nouns
b2plus-nominalization.pattern: -tion/-ment/-té/-esse (verb/adjective → noun), common in formal and written French
b2plus-nominalization.explanation: Formal and written French favors nouns where everyday speech uses verbs: instead of "nous avons décidé vite" (we decided quickly), a report might say "la rapidité de la décision" (the speed of the decision). Common noun-forming suffixes: "-tion" (construire → construction), "-ment" (changer → changement), "-té" (possible → possibilité), "-esse" (triste → tristesse). Recognizing these patterns unlocks a huge amount of formal vocabulary at once, since most of these nouns are entirely predictable from a verb or adjective you already know.
b2plus-nominalization.fact: This nominal style is sometimes criticized in French style guides as "style nominal" when overused — writers are taught that a strong verb ("ils ont décidé vite") often reads better than its noun version ("il y a eu rapidité dans la décision"), even though both are grammatically correct.
